name: Certainty effect
statement: People overweight outcomes they treat as certain, so a sure prize beats a better gamble, and the preference flips when the same pair is made uncertain.
meaning: Maurice Allais posed two questions. The first sets a sure sum against a gamble that pays five times as much with probability 0.1, the sure sum with probability 0.89 and nothing with probability 0.01. The second strips a 0.89 chance of the middle prize out of both options, leaving the middle prize at probability 0.11 against the large prize at probability 0.1. Expected utility theory says the answers must agree, because the same slice was removed from both sides. Most respondents take the certain sum in the first question and the riskier option in the second, which no utility function permits. Two designs generate the pattern. The common-consequence version removes a shared outcome from both prospects, and is the classic Allais paradox. The common-ratio version scales both probabilities down by one factor, as in a choice between 3,000 for sure and 4,000 at probability 0.8, then between the same prizes at 0.25 and 0.2. A pair of questions admits four answer patterns, two consistent with the theory and two not. The two inconsistent ones are called fanning out and fanning in, and the paradox is the claim that fanning out is both common and the more common of the two.

origin.note: "Le Comportement de l'Homme Rationnel devant le Risque" set out the example as a thought experiment rather than an experiment, in French francs of 100 million and 500 million. The paper was not opened for this entry and that description is taken from Blavatskyy, Ortmann and Panchenko, who cite Allais 1953 at pages 527 and 529. Huck and Müller record that Allais put the questions to Leonard Savage with the sums purely hypothetical. The name "certainty effect" is Kahneman and Tversky's, from their 1979 prospect theory paper in the same journal.

evidence: Kahneman and Tversky ran the Allais questions on students and university faculty as hypothetical choices in Israeli pounds. In their Problem 1, 82 per cent of 72 respondents took 2,400 for certain over a gamble paying 2,500 at probability 0.33, 2,400 at 0.66 and nothing at 0.01. In Problem 2, 83 per cent of the same 72 took 2,500 at probability 0.33 over 2,400 at 0.34. They report that 61 per cent of respondents made the modal choice in both, and each preference was significant at the .01 level. Their common-ratio pair moved 95 respondents from 80 per cent choosing 3,000 for sure over 4,000 at 0.8, to 65 per cent choosing 4,000 at 0.2 over 3,000 at 0.25. A non-monetary pair using tours of Europe gave 78 per cent and 67 per cent among 72 respondents. Huck and Müller put the same two questions to the CentERpanel, a representative sample of Dutch households. Of 1,676 members who logged on, 1,426 took part, split across three between-subject treatments: high hypothetical payoffs of nothing, one million and five million euros; low hypothetical payoffs of nothing, five and twenty-five euros; and the same low payoffs paid for real. Violation rates in their Table 2 were 49.4 per cent of 401 at the high hypothetical stakes, 21.2 per cent of 501 at the low hypothetical ones and 25.6 per cent of 524 at the low real ones. The drop from high to low hypothetical stakes gave Conlisk's D statistic of 9.115, p < 0.0001. They ran the identical design on 223 students in the laboratory in December 2006 and found 35.7 per cent, 5.1 per cent and 8.2 per cent violations across the same three treatments. In every treatment of both samples the fanning-out answer outnumbered the fanning-in answer at p < 0.001 on Conlisk's Z statistic. Conlisk's own 1989 test of the basic version with large hypothetical sums is quoted by Huck and Müller as giving 43.6 per cent fanning out, 6.8 per cent fanning in and 50.4 per cent violations in total. His pilot with small real outcomes found almost no violations, a result reported here from Blavatskyy, Ortmann and Panchenko's account of his appendix rather than from the paper.

replication.headline: The paradox holds up when the sums are large and imaginary, and across 81 published designs it appeared in fewer than half and ran backwards in a fifth.
replication.detail: Blavatskyy, Ortmann and Panchenko re-analysed the raw choices from 81 experiments reported in 29 published articles. Their own later paper describes that dataset as 8,947 observations and counts the outcomes: the standard Allais paradox in 38 designs, or 46.9 per cent, no paradox in 27 designs, or 33.3 per cent, and the reverse paradox, with fanning in outnumbering fanning out, in the remaining 16 designs, or 19.8 per cent. Six design choices predict which of the three a study will find. In the manuscript version hosted by the American Economic Association, which counts 83 experiments and 9,152 observations rather than the published 81, hypothetical incentives raise the probability of a fanning-out answer by 0.098, and presenting the options as simple lotteries rather than in compound or frequency form raises it by 0.135. Under hypothetical incentives fanning out outnumbers fanning in by roughly three to one, and under real incentives the ordering reverses, with fanning in modestly ahead. Real incentives raise the probability of the risk-averse answer consistent with the theory by 0.146. Nine of the 83 experiments cannot reject the hypothesis that subjects were choosing at random among the four patterns. The same team ran the exercise on the common-ratio version, using 143 designs from 39 articles and 14,909 observations. There the effect fared better: the standard common-ratio effect appeared in 85 designs, or 59.4 per cent, no effect in 43, or 30.1 per cent, and the reverse in 15, or 10.5 per cent. Cutting the common ratio from the median 0.25 to the 0.01 of Allais's own example raises the chance of seeing the effect by about 0.13. Raising real payoffs cuts it, by 0.054 for each relative increase, while raising hypothetical payoffs adds 0.011. Against the sceptical reading sits a direct multinational replication. Ruggeri and 31 colleagues put 17 of Kahneman and Tversky's 20 items to 4,099 people in 19 countries and 13 languages, with values converted to local currency and the choices left hypothetical. Sixteen of the 17 items replicated in the pooled data at a threshold of .0001, and 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated. Seventy-seven per cent of the country-level effects were smaller than in 1979. The one pooled item indistinguishable from chance was item 4, the second question of the common-ratio pair, at p = .14.

study.cite: Blavatskyy, P., Ortmann, A., & Panchenko, V. (2022). On the experimental robustness of the Allais paradox. American Economic Journal: Microeconomics, 14(1), 143-163.

limits: The record has no preregistered multi-site test of the Allais questions with real money at stakes anyone would call large, and there cannot be one, because the original question offers a million. Every incentivised test therefore scales the prizes down, which is itself the manipulation that weakens the effect. Huck and Müller's own paper disagrees with itself on one figure: their Table 2 gives 21.2 per cent violations in the low hypothetical treatment, their text gives 19.6 per cent, and the table is what is reported above. Their result also cuts against two earlier studies. Moving from small hypothetical to small real payoffs raised violations slightly in their panel, D = -1.6716, p = 0.047, where Harrison and Burke and colleagues had found real payoffs reducing them. Conlisk's 1989 paper was not obtained, and both figures attributed to it here come through later authors. The count in the Allais meta-study depends on which version is read, 81 experiments in the published abstract against 83 in the manuscript, and the 8,947 observations quoted above come from the authors' own restatement in 2023 rather than from the 2022 article. Bruhin, Fehr-Duda and Epper's Econometrica study is often cited nearby and does not test this: they elicited certainty equivalents from 448 subjects in Zurich and Beijing over nearly 18,000 real-money decisions, but the probabilities on offer ran from 5 to 95 per cent, so no option was ever certain. What they found is that about 20 per cent of subjects weight probabilities near linearly and behave as expected value maximisers, around 30 per cent depart sharply from linear weighting and the remaining half depart mildly. That is evidence about the weighting function, not about the sure thing.
misreadings: The version everyone meets is the version most likely to produce the effect. Hypothetical money, prizes in the millions, a middle outcome sitting close to the highest one, options laid out as simple probability distributions, and probability mass split 0.1 against 0.01 rather than evenly. Each of those is a positive predictor in the meta-study, and a design that drops them can produce no paradox or the reverse of it. Quoting the original alongside a modern incentivised result as though they measured the same thing is the common error. A second error is reading the headline percentages as violation rates. The 82 and 83 per cent in Kahneman and Tversky are the shares choosing each modal option separately, and the share of individuals who made both modal choices, which is what violates the theory, is 61 per cent. A third is treating the common-ratio and common-consequence versions as one finding. They are separate designs with separate records, and the common-ratio version survives its meta-study better than the Allais paradox survives its own. Some papers report common-ratio experiments under the name Allais paradox, which is how the two literatures get merged. Whether certainty is doing the work is also contested. Incekara-Hafalir, Kim and Stecher argue from laboratory evidence that the driver is aversion to receiving nothing rather than the appeal of a sure thing, and describe the evidence for the certainty effect as weak to nonexistent; their full text was not obtained and that is their abstract's wording. Finally, the certainty effect is the half of prospect theory that concerns probability weighting, and is a different claim from the kink in the value function. The loss aversion entry covers that half and the argument over its coefficient.
